subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Wisdom (and Madness) of Crowds
description: A quick win: understand The Wisdom (and Madness) of Crowds.

hook.text: In 1906, Francis Galton found that 787 people guessing an ox's weight averaged 1,198 lbs. The actual weight: 1,198 lbs.

buildup.text: The wisdom of crowds: aggregated independent judgments often outperform individual experts.

discovery.text: Three conditions make crowds wise: diversity of opinion, independence of judgment, and decentralized information.

twist.text: Remove any condition and crowds become mad: groupthink, information cascades, bubbles, and panics.

climax.text: Markets, prediction platforms, and Wikipedia all harness crowd wisdom. Social media often destroys it.

punchline.text: Crowds are wise when they think independently. Mobs think together.

quiz.question: What conditions are needed for crowds to be wise?
options: Diversity of opinion, independence of judgment, and decentralized information

details.summary: Crowds can be remarkably accurate when members think independently, have diverse perspectives, and are decentralized. When these conditions fail, crowds become mobs that amplify error instead of averaging it out.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing when crowds are wise and when they are dangerous helps you decide whether to follow group judgment or trust your own analysis.
takeaways: Independent diverse crowds often outperform individual experts
Social influence destroys crowd wisdom by creating correlation
James Surowiecki identified four conditions for wise crowds

faq.question: What conditions are necessary for a crowd to produce wise judgments?
faq.answer: Surowiecki identified four: diversity of opinion, independence of members, decentralization (people draw on local knowledge), and a mechanism for aggregating individual judgments. Remove any one and crowd wisdom collapses.

faq.question: How can social media undermine the wisdom of crowds?
faq.answer: Social media destroys independence by letting people see others' opinions before forming their own. This creates herding, where early opinions cascade into consensus that reflects the first movers, not genuine collective intelligence.
